key_facts: Sudden crops of small yellow papules with a red rim on the buttocks, elbows or knees, often in poorly controlled diabetes.
Very high triglycerides leak into the dermis and are taken up by macrophages.

Acute pancreatitis (triglycerides >10–20 mmol/L); familial hypercholesterolaemia with tendon xanthomas.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: Crops of small (1–5 mm) **yellow papules with a red halo**, appearing over weeks, on the **buttocks**, extensor arms/thighs and shoulders. They are the skin marker of **severe hypertriglyceridaemia** (usually TG **>10–20 mmol/L**, chylomicronaemia).

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: Excess circulating **chylomicrons/VLDL** leak through dermal capillaries and are taken up by macrophages (foam cells), with **extracellular lipid** deposits early on.

ul: **Secondary causes:** **uncontrolled diabetes** (insulin deficiency → less lipoprotein lipase activity — this case: fasting glucose 18.1); **obesity**/metabolic syndrome (BMI 35); **alcohol**; hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, CKD, pregnancy; **drugs:** oral oestrogens, tamoxifen, **retinoids (isotretinoin, acitretin)**, corticosteroids, thiazides, β-blockers, **ciclosporin/tacrolimus/sirolimus**, protease inhibitors, **atypical antipsychotics** (olanzapine, clozapine), propofol, L-asparaginase
**Primary:** familial chylomicronaemia syndrome (LPL deficiency), multifactorial chylomicronaemia, familial hypertriglyceridaemia, dysbetalipoproteinaemia.

sections.title: Clinical features
blocks: Clusters of firm, non-tender or slightly itchy yellow-orange papules with erythematous bases; Koebnerisation. Larger coalescing (tubero-eruptive) lesions with persistent disease. Look also for **lipaemia retinalis** (creamy retinal vessels), hepatosplenomegaly, abdominal pain (**pancreatitis**). Other xanthoma types point to other lipid disorders: tendon (FH), tuberous (elbows/knees — dysbetalipoproteinaemia/FH), palmar crease (dysbetalipoproteinaemia), xanthelasma (half have normal lipids).

ul: **Fasting lipid profile.** The sample is **turbid/milky ("lipaemic")** with **very high TG**. Cholesterol is also raised.
**HbA1c**, glucose, U&E/eGFR, LFT (fatty liver, alcohol), **TSH**, urine ACR/PCR, amylase/lipase if abdominal pain.
**Shave or punch biopsy** only if uncertain (foamy macrophages ± extracellular lipid).

**NICE NG238 (2023):** **TG >20 mmol/L** (not caused by excess alcohol or poor glycaemic control) → **urgent specialist referral**; **TG 10–20 mmol/L** → **repeat fasting TG within 5–14 days**, review and treat secondary causes; **seek specialist advice if still >10**; In practice, a TG >20 with xanthomas and new diabetes needs **urgent** management whatever the cause, because of pancreatitis risk

sections.title: Differential diagnoses
blocks: **Molluscum contagiosum** (umbilicated, pearly), **dermatitis herpetiformis** (itchy grouped excoriated papules/vesicles, same sites), folliculitis/acne, **papular granuloma annulare**, xanthoma disseminatum/non-Langerhans histiocytosis, papular sarcoid, milia, insect bites, juvenile xanthogranuloma.

sections.title: Management

ol: **Treat the diabetes promptly** (NICE NG28). A fasting glucose of 18.1 with a new diagnosis needs HbA1c and ketones. With symptomatic hyperglycaemia or very high TG, **insulin** (or a sulfonylurea) achieves rapid control and rapidly lowers TG. Then metformin ± SGLT2 inhibitor/GLP-1 RA for long-term control and weight.
**Stop alcohol** completely while TG is very high. **Review culprit drugs** (oestrogens, thiazides, β-blockers, retinoids, antipsychotics, steroids).
**Dietitian:** very-low-fat diet (<10–15% energy from fat) for chylomicronaemia; avoid simple sugars; weight loss.

**Lipid-lowering:** **Fenofibrate** (specialist-advised) when TG remains >10 mmol/L despite control of secondary causes, to reduce **pancreatitis** risk; **Statin** for CVD risk — **atorvastatin 20 mg** for primary prevention in T2DM if QRISK3 ≥10%; **Icosapent ethyl** (NICE TA805) for secondary prevention with raised TG on statins
**Xanthomas regress** within weeks to months of TG control — a useful motivator.
**Safety-net for pancreatitis:** severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, vomiting → ED.

blocks: Within diabetes/lipid IP competence: start diabetes therapy (incl. insulin if trained), statin, stop alcohol/culprit drugs, arrange repeat lipids, refer urgently per NG238. Fibrate/specialist therapies as advised.

refer.t: Triglycerides above 20 mmol/L: **urgent specialist referral** (NICE NG238); abdominal pain raises concern for **acute pancreatitis**, same-day assessment.
Tendon xanthomas or xanthelasma in a young person: check for **familial hypercholesterolaemia** (NICE CG71).

blocks: Abdominal pain (pancreatitis — same day); TG >20 mmol/L (urgent lipid clinic); TG >10 persistently; suspected familial chylomicronaemia (onset in childhood, recurrent pancreatitis); DKA/HHS features (glucose 18 + vomiting/ketones).

pearls: "**Yellow papules on the buttocks in new diabetes = check triglycerides today — pancreatitis risk.**"
Before starting **isotretinoin, acitretin or oral oestrogen**, check fasting lipids if there are risk factors (family history, obesity, diabetes, alcohol).
